seo_title: Declining Results: The Person or the Method? — SIT™
title: When Results Drop: Is It the Person, or the Method?
content:
###  **Both Answers Are Sometimes Right** 

When marketing results decline, there are two possible explanations, and companies tend to reach for the same one every time. 

Sometimes the person is genuinely the problem. In work that depends on human interaction, individual performance varies enormously — two field representatives working the same street on the same day can produce results that differ by a factor of three. That is precisely why we are selective about who we hire, and why we replace people who are not performing. 

But sometimes the method itself has aged out, and no amount of individual effort would have changed the outcome. Reaching for the first explanation when the second is true costs a company far more than the mistake appears to. 

###  **How to Tell Which One You Are Looking At** 

The useful test is whether the role has a meaningful performance range. 

A conversation has enormous range. How someone opens, whether they read the homeowner correctly, whether they are comfortable enough that the other person relaxes — all of that changes the outcome dramatically. When conversation-based outreach underperforms, the individual is a legitimate suspect. 

Delivering printed material has almost no range. The paper is on the door or it is not. There is no version of that job done exceptionally well that overcomes a channel homeowners have stopped reading. 

###  **A Company That Got This Wrong** 

A family landscaping business, more than three decades old and generational, had relied on door hangers for years. It worked for a long time. Then response fell off. 

The owner concluded that the person delivering them had stopped doing the work, and let him go. 

We did not think that was what happened, and said so directly. Door hangers have declined broadly, for a reason that has nothing to do with delivery: homeowners have learned to remove and discard them without reading. The message is never evaluated at all. 

The person was almost certainly doing the job. The job had stopped working. 

###  **The Second Half of the Story** 

We ran conversations for that company instead, starting in late October in Wisconsin. Homeowners talked, and most of them wanted to be contacted in spring — which is what late-autumn outreach in a northern climate produces. We also brought back what those homeowners said, including feedback from past customers and people who had taken their quotes and gone elsewhere. 

That feedback was not something they wanted. The expectation was immediate sales, and interest scheduled for spring did not count. 

###  **The Two Lessons** 

First: before deciding who is responsible for a decline, check whether the role in question even has the range to be responsible. Replacing someone in a job with no performance range changes nothing and costs a quarter. 

Second: feedback only helps a company willing to change something because of it. 

###  **Where That Leaves Us** 

The same test applies to our own work, and it cuts against us rather than for us. Field conversations have enormous performance range, which means when our results are weak, our people genuinely are a legitimate explanation. The method is not our defense — that is what the commitment in our agreements is for.
